ta-l1d24q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 24 turns to names annexed to plurality and announces two articles: on those related to plurality as its principle, and on the name 'Trinity', which follows plurality as a quasi-collective.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that there is diversity in God. As one in substance makes the same, multitude in substance makes the diverse, and Hilary says the three are three by substance and one by harmony.
claims: Hilary says the persons are three by substance.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. As one is said from not being divided, many are said from being divided, and Father and Son are several, so there is division in God.
claims: Plurality implies division.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument. 'Alien' (alienus) is named from 'other' (alius), and the Son is other than the Father, so he can be called alien.
claims: Alienus derives from alius.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument that the Father can be called singular. 'Singular' signifies something designated subsisting in a common nature, as the Father is, so Damascene (Dist. 19) says he is like an individual.
claims: The Father is like an individual.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e122.summary: Fifth argument that God can be called unique (unicus), since the Church sings of proclaiming God triune and unique.
claims: The liturgy calls God unicus.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e128.summary: Sixth argument that there cannot be discreteness in God, since 'discrete' is a difference of quantity and there is no quantity in God.
claims: Discreteness is a difference of quantity.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e131.summary: The general question is posed: which of these terms can be granted of God.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e134.summary: Thomas's determination. There were two heresies about the Trinity, Arius introducing a plurality of essence and Sabellius removing the plurality of persons, and the Catholic faith grants what each denied, so we must grant what opposes both heresies and deny what accords with either. Against Arius the Church posits four things: unity of essence, so it confesses God one and denies diversity; simplicity of the divine essence, so it confesses him simple and denies multiplicity, division (which implies whole and part), and separation; likeness in the nature of deity signified as a form, so it calls the Son like the Father and denies 'alien', which means foreign to someone's nature; and the undivided power and greatness of the three persons, so it says 'equal' and denies 'unequal' or 'disparate'. Against Sabellius it also posits four: communication of nature to several supposits, so it affirms plurality and excludes singularity; that this plurality is real and not merely conceptual, since there are three things, so it affirms distinction and excludes 'unique'; an order of origin among the persons, so it affirms discreteness, which implies order, and excludes confusion; and that the three persons are united by a fellowship of love, the Holy Spirit, so it affirms harmony (Hilary) and excludes solitude.
claims: Admissible terms are those opposed to both Arianism and Sabellianism.
Against Arius: unity, simplicity, likeness, equality; denying diversity, division, alienness, inequality.
Against Sabellius: plurality, real distinction, order, harmony; denying singularity, uniqueness, confusion, solitude.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the first argument. One in substance, meaning essence, makes the same, and multitude in substance, meaning essence, makes the diverse, but Hilary in saying 'three by substance' takes substance for hypostasis, not essence.
claims: Hilary's 'substance' means hypostasis.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the second argument. Where there is number simply there is division by essence or quantity, but in God there is only a certain number, for which distinction of relations suffices.
claims: Distinction of relations suffices for divine number.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e144.summary: Reply to the third argument. The Son is called other (alius) than the Father but not alien (alienus), since 'alien' implies foreignness of nature; it is named from otherness of nature, not of supposit.
claims: Alienus implies otherness of nature, alius only of supposit.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e147.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A divine person cannot properly be called singular, since the singular is that whose essence is incommunicable, and the Father's essence is not incommunicable.
claims: Singularity requires incommunicable essence.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e150.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. For the stated reason, God cannot be called unique (unicus); where it is found, 'unicus' is used improperly for 'unus', and all such authorities should be glossed accordingly.
claims: 'Unicus' said of God is improper for 'unus'.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e153.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Discreteness is preserved in God not by the character of quantity but only by that of order.
claims: Divine discreteness is by order, not quantity.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e156.summary: The answer to the general question is clear from what has been said.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e168.summary: First argument that 'Trinity' is an essential name. Whatever is not referred to another is essential, and 'Trinity' by its name is not.
claims: 'Trinity' is not a relative name.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e171.summary: Second argument. What is predicated of each person and of all together singularly is essential. 'Trinity' is said as 'unity of three', and that unity signifies the essence, so since the Father is the essence and the unity of the essence, he is the unity of three, i.e. the Trinity, as are Son and Spirit, and the three are one Trinity, not several.
claims: Trinitas as trium unitas would be predicated of each person.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e174.summary: Third argument, against the reply that 'Trinity' is a collective of the persons. Bernard says the unity of the Trinity holds the summit among all unities, but the unity implied by a collective name is the least of unities, so 'Trinity' is not collective and in no way signifies relation.
claims: The Trinity's unity is the highest; collective unity is the lowest.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e178.summary: Sed contra from Boethius, who says the name 'Trinity' pertains to relation.
claims: 'Trinity' pertains to relation.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e181.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Trinity' implies unity and a certain number, and unity in God is essential or personal. Some say it implies personal unity, expounding 'Trinitas' as 'ter unitas', three personal unities, so that it signifies relation absolutely. Others say the unity is essential, expounding it as 'trium unitas', as Isidore does in the text. This seems more fitting, since from 'Trinity' we call God 'trinus', and he cannot be called 'three times one', since 'one God' signifies essential unity. So 'Trinity' signifies both the unity of essence and the distinction of persons.
claims: 'Trinity' signifies both unity of essence and distinction of persons.
Trinitas is better expounded as trium unitas than ter unitas.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e184.summary: Reply to the first argument. As to what it is imposed to signify, 'Trinity' signifies not relation but number, so by its name it is not referred to another, but as to what this number in God is about, it signifies the relations themselves, which alone are numbered in God. It adds nothing in reality, only the character of negation (q. 1, a. 3). Being relative belongs to the Trinity not as Trinity but as divine Trinity, so it has an implicit relation.
claims: 'Trinity' signifies number, which in God concerns the relations, so it has an implicit relation.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e187.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'The Father is the Trinity' is false. Although, by its abstract mode of signifying and its etymology ('trium unitas'), 'Trinity' signifies unity of essence directly and number of persons obliquely, by its imposition it is the reverse: it is imposed from the number it implies. So in its true signification 'Trinity' means 'three persons of one essence', as Lombard explains, and the Father cannot be called the Trinity. Likewise 'God is triune' means he has three persons in one essence, with 'God' standing for the essence or an undistinguished supposit.
claims: 'The Father is the Trinity' is false.
By imposition 'Trinity' signifies three persons of one essence.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e190.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Trinity' resembles a collective name but is not truly one. A collective involves a multitude of things simply divided by essence and the least unity in which they are gathered. In 'Trinity' it is the reverse: what gathers the three persons is the greatest unity, of essence, and the persons gathered have the least of real multitude. There is still a likeness, since both involve a number and a unity, which is why Lombard (Dist. 19) called it quasi-collective.
claims: 'Trinity' is quasi-collective: maximal unity gathering minimal multitude.

ta-l1d24q2-d1e199.summary: An expositio textus. 'Since there is neither number nor quantity there' shows Lombard means that unity and multitude predicate something added to their subjects only as in the genus of quantity, and in that way they are not predicated of God. 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' was expounded in Dist. 2.
claims: Unity and multitude add something only as quantitative, which does not apply to God.

ta-l1d24q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two articles on names annexed to plurality: those related to it as principle, and 'Trinity' as quasi-collective.

ta-l1d24q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks which terms related to plurality can be granted of God. Thomas's rule is to grant what opposes both Arius and Sabellius and deny what accords with either. Against Arius the Church affirms unity, simplicity, likeness, and equality, denying diversity, division, alienness, and inequality; against Sabellius it affirms plurality, real distinction, order of origin, and harmony, denying singularity, uniqueness, confusion, and solitude. Hilary's 'three by substance' means hypostasis; the Son is other but not alien; no person is singular since the essence is communicable; 'unicus' is improper; and discreteness holds by order, not quantity.
claims: Trinitarian terms are admitted or excluded by opposition to Arius and Sabellius.
Discreteness in God is by order; no person is singular.

ta-l1d24q2-Dd1e160.summary: Article 2 asks whether 'Trinity' is an essential name. It signifies both unity of essence and distinction of persons, better expounded as 'trium unitas'. By imposition it signifies the number of persons, three persons of one essence, so it has an implicit relation and 'the Father is the Trinity' is false. It is quasi-collective, gathering the least real multitude in the greatest unity.
claims: 'Trinity' signifies three persons of one essence and is not predicated of a single person.
It is quasi-collective, not truly collective.

ta-l1d24q2-Dd1e194.summary: The Expositio textus notes that unity and multitude add something to their subjects only as quantitative, and so are not predicated of God in that way.
claims: Quantitative unity and multitude do not apply to God.

ta-l1d24q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 24 treats names annexed to plurality. Article 1 sets out the rule for Trinitarian language: grant what opposes both Arius and Sabellius and deny what agrees with either. So the Church affirms unity, simplicity, likeness, and equality of essence, and plurality, real distinction, order of origin, and harmony of persons. It denies diversity, division, alienness, and inequality, and also singularity, uniqueness, confusion, and solitude. Article 2 holds that 'Trinity' signifies both unity of essence and distinction of persons. By imposition it means three persons of one essence, so it is not said of any single person, and it is only quasi-collective.
claims: Trinitarian terms are governed by opposition to Arianism and Sabellianism.
'Trinity' means three persons of one essence and is quasi-collective.
